question: What changes across two decades of one pianist’s nocturne?
intro: Paderewski recorded this nocturne in London on30 January 1937, two decades after the Victor performance also in the comparison. His own 1909 essay treats rubato as expressive flexibility, not a debt that must always be repaid later in the bar. That is documented context for listening, not permission to invent a timed gesture.

cues.title: Rubato on his own terms
cues.text: Paderewski wrote that time taken from a phrase need not be paid back mechanically. Listen for the larger line rather than using a metronome as the sole judge of his 1937 performance.

cues.title: The central departure
cues.text: A pair of strong measured changes occurs around 1:26–1:30, followed by the recording’s largest change at 1:46. Hear the growing contrast as a span rather than a single precisely timed pivot.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-nocturne-op15-2-paderewski-1937.txt: novelty86, 90, 106 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: The crest arrives later
cues.text: The highest five-second average level occurs around 2:05. Compare the spacing of the approach with the 1917 performance rather than calling either one simply faster throughout.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-nocturne-op15-2-paderewski-1937.txt: highest level125 seconds; neighbouring high windows110–120 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: The late turn
cues.text: A strong measured change introduces the closing region. The transfer then falls towards its quiet ending; its noise floor cannot tell us exactly when the pianist released the pedal.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
